subject: mathematics
question_text: In a △ABC, prove that (1 + cos(A−B) cos C)/(1 + cos(A−C) cos B) = (a² + b²)/(a² + c²).

mark_split.label: Replace C and B using the angle sum

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.111 — from the book's separate "STAR QUESTIONS PLUS" bank, answer 178, under its "PROPERTIES OF TRIANGLES" heading. That bank (book pp.98-111, answers 142-180) sits AFTER all the numbered chapters and is organised by chapter rather than being part of any chapter's inventory; it is authored into this unit because that is where the question belongs on the paper. ⚠ IT CARRIES NO MARK CUT. The Star Questions Plus headings name the chapter but not the section, so this answer is classed as an SAQ on its length and shape — it is comparable to answers 80-87 in the Properties of Triangles SAQ chapter — and that classification is OURS, not the book's. Printed appearances: AP 19. The angle C appears only as cos C, and in a triangle cos C = −cos(A+B) — which turns each numerator into a difference of two cosines and then into a difference of squares. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — no [N Marks] tags are printed against this answer. It is not a bare guess: the same book prints 1+1+1+1 for the 4-mark answers 58 and 59 on book p.63 and 1+2+1 for answer 61 on p.64, so both shapes used in this unit are the book's own. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — name each standard result you use and the order you use them in.

steps.label: Replace C and B using the angle sum
steps.margin_note: Half the marks. In a triangle C = 180° − (A+B), so cos C = −cos(A+B). The same applies to cos B in the denominator.

recall.must_convey: That cos C = −cos(A+B) and cos B = −cos(A+C), turning both plus signs into minus signs.
accept: in a triangle cos C is minus cos of A plus B so the plus becomes a minus in both numerator and denominator
use the angle sum to replace cos C and cos B
both signs flip because cosine changes sign across one eighty
cos C ante minus cos A plus B, so signs marutai

steps.why: The whole identity depends on this substitution — without it there is no way to combine cos(A−B) with cos C at all.

steps.label: Use the product identity
steps.margin_note: Third mark. cos(A+B)cos(A−B) = cos²A − sin²B — the standard product result, which turns each bracket into squares.

recall.must_convey: That cos(A+B)cos(A−B) = cos²A − sin²B is applied and 1 − cos²A = sin²A, giving (sin²A+sin²B)/(sin²A+sin²C).
accept: use cos A plus B times cos A minus B equals cos squared A minus sin squared B then one minus cos squared A is sin squared A
the brackets become sums of sine squares
it reduces to sin squared A plus sin squared B over sin squared A plus sin squared C
product identity vaadi, sines ga marchali
apply the product formula and the Pythagorean identity
heard_as: cos squared A minus sin squared B

steps.why: Two identities in one line: the product formula makes squares, and 1 − cos² makes them all sines. After this everything is in sines and the sine rule can finish it.
common_mistakes: Losing the sign when distributing the minus.

steps.label: Apply the sine rule
steps.margin_note: Last mark. a = 2R sinA, so sinA = a/(2R) — and the (2R)² cancels top and bottom, leaving the sides.
lines: By the sine rule, sinA = a/2R, sinB = b/2R, sinC = c/2R

recall.must_convey: That the sine rule replaces each sine by side/(2R), and the 4R² cancels to leave (a²+b²)/(a²+c²).
accept: use the sine rule so each sine is a side over two R and the four R squared cancels leaving the sides
the sine rule converts the sines into sides
four R squared cancels top and bottom
sine rule tho sines ni sides ga marchite four R square cancel avthundi

steps.why: Both numerator and denominator carry the same 4R², so it cancels completely — which is why the answer has no R in it despite the sine rule being used.
common_mistakes: Cancelling only one of the two.
